title: Repeated digits, palindromes and repunits
transcript: A palindrome reads the same from either end. Matching digits sit in paired places on either side of its centre. A repunit is made entirely of ones. Place value lets us build a repeated digit with one multiplication.

In AMC Upper Primary practice, watch for numbers that read the same when reversed, or a long row of repeated digits. In a Rossmoyne style puzzle, add a divisibility rule. Use the mirror structure to leave fewer free choices.
Take the repunit one thousand one hundred and eleven and multiply by four. What number will you get? Picture multiplying each place separately. Look for any place that would need a carry.

Each one becomes a four. The product in every column is below ten, so no digit has to move into the next place. The answer is four thousand four hundred and forty-four. You can view it as one copy of that digit in every position.
The four-digit number three thousand six hundred and sixty-three reads the same both ways. Divide it by eleven. Can you find the quotient by splitting the outer and inner pairs of digits?

The two outer copies of three contribute three thousand and three. The two inner copies of six contribute six hundred and sixty. One thousand and one is eleven times ninety-one. One hundred and ten is eleven times ten. Both pairs share a factor of eleven. Now add ninety-one times three and ten times six. The quotient is three hundred and thirty-three.

Count the five-digit palindromes divisible by nine whose first digit is at most five. The first and last digits match. So do the second and fourth. The centre can be any single digit allowed by the divisibility test.

A five-digit palindrome is fixed once we choose its first two digits and the centre. Call them A, B and C. The digit sum is twice A plus twice B plus C. For each outer pair choose C to make the sum a multiple of nine. There is always a choice from zero through eight, since those digits give all nine remainders. Nine is a second choice precisely when zero already worked. That happens when A plus B is itself divisible by nine.

The pair can sum to nine, with one partner from zero to eight for each allowed first digit. A sum of eighteen is outside our permitted range. Add fifty and five. The answer is fifty-five, with each number counted once by its three free positions.

Starting with zero would give fewer than five written digits. Only the centre and the second digit may start from zero in this count. When the required remainder is zero, both zero and nine work as centre digits. Test those two endpoints before you count.
Write only the independent digits first. Use the mirror pairs to copy the other positions. Use the divisibility test on the resulting digit sum. Check whether the residue allows two single digits.
